claim: Lung squamous cell carcinoma (LUSC) accounts for 20–30% of all lung cancer cases.
source: Lung squamous cell carcinoma (LUSC) is a type of non-small cell lung cancer that accounts for 20–30% of all lung cancer cases (Chen et al., 2014; Sung et al., 2021; Bray et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by three citations to published literature (Chen et al., 2014; Sung et al., 2021; Bray et al., 2021).

claim: LUSC is the second most frequent type of lung cancer.
source: Despite being the second most frequent type of lung cancer (Torre et al., 2016), our knowledge regarding the biology of this disease as well as the therapeutic modalities to treat it remain far behind the most frequent type of lung cancer, lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) (Hirsch et al., 2016; Khuder, 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Torre et al., 2016.

claim: LUAD genetics is dominated by mutations that activate the RTK/RAS pathway, including EGFR and KRAS mutations.
source: LUAD genetics is dominated by mutations (that are often druggable) that activate the RTK/RAS pathway, including EGFR and KRAS mutations (The Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network, 2012; Jamal-Hanjani et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two published studies (The Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network, 2012; Jamal-Hanjani et al., 2017).

claim: The genetic landscape of LUSC is more complex than LUAD, with multiple pathways altered in subsets of patients and a lack of actionable mutations.
source: However, the genetic landscape of LUSC is more complex, with multiple pathways altered in subsets of patients and a lack of actionable mutations (Campbell et al., 2016; The Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network, 2012; Kim et al., 2014), precluding the development of new therapies.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to three published studies (Campbell et al., 2016; The Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network, 2012; Kim et al., 2014).

claim: The only pharmacological therapies available to treat LUSC patients are immune checkpoint inhibitor monotherapy or in combination with chemotherapy.
source: Hence, the only pharmacological therapies available to treat LUSC patients are immune checkpoint inhibitor monotherapy or in combination with chemotherapy (Mok et al., 2019; Paz-Ares et al., 2018; Weinberg and Gadgeel, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to three published studies (Mok et al., 2019; Paz-Ares et al., 2018; Weinberg and Gadgeel, 2019).

claim: The National Lung Cancer Matrix Trial and The Lung Master Protocol have not shown clear therapeutic benefits with targeted agents in LUSC.
source: Furthermore, the National Lung Cancer Matrix Trial and The Lung Master Protocol, the largest personalized medicine trials in lung cancer, have not shown clear therapeutic benefits with targeted agents in LUSC (; Middleton et al., 2020; Redman et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two published studies (Middleton et al., 2020; Redman et al., 2020).

claim: LUSC has a worse prognosis than LUAD independent of stage at detection.
source: LUSC also has a worse prognosis than LUAD independent of stage at detection, with a 5-year overall survival (OS) of 6.2% for patients diagnosed with distant metastasis (9.5% for LUAD).
evidence: The claim is supported by specific survival statistics provided in the text.

claim: The 5-year overall survival for LUSC patients diagnosed with distant metastasis is 6.2%.
source: LUSC also has a worse prognosis than LUAD independent of stage at detection, with a 5-year overall survival (OS) of 6.2% for patients diagnosed with distant metastasis (9.5% for LUAD).
evidence: The claim is supported by specific survival data presented in the text.

claim: The 5-year overall survival for LUAD patients diagnosed with distant metastasis is 9.5%.
source: LUSC also has a worse prognosis than LUAD independent of stage at detection, with a 5-year overall survival (OS) of 6.2% for patients diagnosed with distant metastasis (9.5% for LUAD).
evidence: The claim is supported by specific survival data presented in the text.

claim: The 5-year overall survival for LUSC patients diagnosed with localized disease is 50%.
source: However, patients diagnosed with localized disease are eligible for curative surgery and the 5-year OS is 50% (National Cancer Institute and DCCPS, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by specific survival data and a citation to National Cancer Institute and DCCPS, 2018.

claim: 40% of early diagnosed LUSC patients die within 5 years despite detection of localized lung cancer eligible for resection with curative intent.
source: These initiatives make use of low-dose CT scans in high-risk populations, but in spite of the frequent detection of localized lung cancer eligible for resection with curative intent, 40% of early diagnosed patients die within 5 years.
evidence: The claim is supported by specific mortality data presented in the text.

claim: LUSC progresses through a series of premalignant stages characterized by alterations of the normal bronchial epithelium.
source: LUSC progresses through a series of premalignant stages characterized by alterations of the normal bronchial epithelium (Figure 1; Ishizumi et al., 2010; Kadara et al., 2016; Thakrar et al., 2017; Pennycuick et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to four published studies (Ishizumi et al., 2010; Kadara et al., 2016; Thakrar et al., 2017; Pennycuick et al., 2020) and reference to Figure 1.

claim: Endobronchial premalignant lesions (PMLs) are classified as low-grade (squamous metaplasia, mild and moderate dysplasia) and high-grade (severe dysplasia, and carcinomas in situ [CIS]).
source: These endobronchial premalignant lesions (PMLs) are classified as low-grade (squamous metaplasia, mild and moderate dysplasia) and high-grade (severe dysplasia, and carcinomas in situ [CIS]) (Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by the text description and reference to Figure 1.

claim: Not all PMLs progress to LUSC.
source: However, not all PMLs progress to LUSC.
evidence: The claim is stated as a fact in the text.

claim: High-grade PMLs have a higher risk of progression than low grade.
source: Although obvious differences exist between the multiple studies published on the topic, high-grade PMLs have a higher risk of progression than low grade, and high levels of chromosomal instability (CIN) are also predictive of progressive PMLs (Thakrar et al., 2017; van Boerdonk et al., 2014; Teixeira et al., 2019; Merrick et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to four published studies (Thakrar et al., 2017; van Boerdonk et al., 2014; Teixeira et al., 2019; Merrick et al., 2016).

claim: High levels of chromosomal instability (CIN) are predictive of progressive PMLs.
source: Although obvious differences exist between the multiple studies published on the topic, high-grade PMLs have a higher risk of progression than low grade, and high levels of chromosomal instability (CIN) are also predictive of progressive PMLs (Thakrar et al., 2017; van Boerdonk et al., 2014; Teixeira et al., 2019; Merrick et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to four published studies (Thakrar et al., 2017; van Boerdonk et al., 2014; Teixeira et al., 2019; Merrick et al., 2016).

claim: CIN has been observed as a potential biomarker of PMLs progression in both low- and high-grade PMLs.
source: This potential role of CIN as biomarker of PMLs progression has been observed in low- and high-grade PMLs (van Boerdonk et al., 2014; Teixeira et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two published studies (van Boerdonk et al., 2014; Teixeira et al., 2019).

claim: High levels of copy number variations was the best predictor of progressive PMLs.
source: These reports showed that high levels of copy number variations was the best predictor of progressive PMLs (van Boerdonk et al., 2014; Teixeira et al., 2019) and that immune response is the most likely cause of regression as these lesions contained higher levels of immune infiltration (Pennycuick et al., 2020; Beane et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two published studies (van Boerdonk et al., 2014; Teixeira et al., 2019).

claim: Immune response is the most likely cause of PML regression as these lesions contained higher levels of immune infiltration.
source: These reports showed that high levels of copy number variations was the best predictor of progressive PMLs (van Boerdonk et al., 2014; Teixeira et al., 2019) and that immune response is the most likely cause of regression as these lesions contained higher levels of immune infiltration (Pennycuick et al., 2020; Beane et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two published studies (Pennycuick et al., 2020; Beane et al., 2019).

claim: Transcriptomic analysis of PMLs indicates immune evasion in the transition to invasiveness.
source: These results are supported by transcriptomic analysis of PMLs that indicate immune evasion in the transition to invasiveness (Mascaux et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Mascaux et al., 2019.

claim: The detection of PMLs cannot be carried out by routine patient imaging techniques such as CT or PET scans.
source: The detection of PMLs cannot be carried out by routine patient imaging techniques such as CT or PET scans as the morphological change that they cause in the airway does not result in radiological contrast.
evidence: The claim is stated as a fact based on the physical properties of PMLs.

claim: Ablation of high-grade PMLs detected by autofluorescence bronchoscopy using minimally invasive endoscopic procedures in high-risk populations is an innovative strategy to prevent LUSC.
source: Alternatively, ablation of high-grade PMLs detected by autofluorescence bronchoscopy using minimally invasive endoscopic procedures in high-risk populations is an innovative and interesting strategy to prevent LUSC (Guibert et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Guibert et al., 2016.

claim: Autofluorescence bronchoscopy is an expensive and complex technique of limited use in large screening programmes.
source: Nonetheless autofluorescence bronchoscopy is an expensive and complex technique of limited use in large screening programmes.
evidence: The claim is stated as a fact about the practical limitations of the technique.

claim: Dataset GSE33479 comprises expression microarray analyses of 122 endobronchial biopsies of unknown progression status.
source: Dataset GSE33479 (Mascaux et al., 2019) comprises expression microarray analyses of 122 endobronchial biopsies of unknown progression status.
evidence: The claim describes the dataset characteristics and is supported by citation to Mascaux et al., 2019.

claim: Dataset GSE109743 consists of a transcriptomic analysis of whole PML biopsies and bronchial brushings obtained from adjacent normal regions of the bronchial mucosa.
source: Dataset GSE109743 (Beane et al., 2019) consists of a transcriptomic analysis of whole PML biopsies with no purification of the epithelial compartment as well as bronchial brushings obtained from adjacent normal regions of the bronchial mucosa.
evidence: The claim describes the dataset characteristics and is supported by citation to Beane et al., 2019.

claim: Dataset GSE109743 used RNAseq and includes the progression status for some lesions established by serial biopsies.
source: Unlike GSE33479, GSE109743 used RNAseq and more importantly, includes the progression status for some lesions established by serial biopsies.
evidence: The claim describes the dataset characteristics.

claim: In dataset GSE109743, samples were classified as 'normal-stable' when they changed between normal, hyperplasia, and metaplasia.
source: Samples were classified as 'normal-stable' when they changed between normal, hyperplasia, and metaplasia, 'regressive' when they regress from dysplasia to a less severe dysplastic grade, or from dysplasia to normal/hyperplasia/metaplasia.
evidence: The claim describes the classification criteria used in the dataset.

claim: In dataset GSE109743, samples were classified as 'regressive' when they regress from dysplasia to a less severe dysplastic grade, or from dysplasia to normal/hyperplasia/metaplasia.
source: Samples were classified as 'normal-stable' when they changed between normal, hyperplasia, and metaplasia, 'regressive' when they regress from dysplasia to a less severe dysplastic grade, or from dysplasia to normal/hyperplasia/metaplasia.
evidence: The claim describes the classification criteria used in the dataset.

claim: Dataset GSE114489 collected 63 baseline bronchial biopsies with corresponding follow-up biopsies.
source: In GSE114489, the authors collected 63 baseline bronchial biopsies (with corresponding follow-up biopsies) and classified samples in four groups: 23 persistent dysplasias (dysplastic lesions with the same or higher severity scores in follow-up biopsies), 15 regressive dysplasias (dysplasias progressing to lower severity scores), 9 progressive non-dysplasias (biopsies with normal or hyperplastic morphologies that progress to more severe morphologies), and 16 stable non-dysplasias (normal or hyperplastic pathology that remains stable in follow-up biopsies).
evidence: The claim describes the dataset characteristics.

claim: Dataset GSE108124 focuses on CIS and progression is defined as the transition to invasive carcinomas in follow-up biopsies.
source: The study published by Teixeira et al., 2019 (GSE108124) also makes use of follow-up biopsies to classify the progression potential of PMLs, but unlike GSE114489, GSE108124 focuses on CIS and progression is defined as the transition to invasive carcinomas in follow-up biopsies.
evidence: The claim describes the dataset characteristics and is supported by citation to Teixeira et al., 2019.

claim: In dataset GSE108124, RNA for gene expression microarray analysis was extracted from microdissected FFPE samples to enrich the epithelial component.
source: RNA for gene expression microarray analysis was extracted from microdissected FFPE samples to enrich the epithelial component.
evidence: The claim describes the methodology used in the dataset.

claim: CIN5 segregates progressive and regressive CIS lesions in cohort GSE108124 with an AUC of 1.
source: Cohort GSE108124 focuses on CIS lesions with known progressive potential. As reported in that study (Teixeira et al., 2019), we found that the CIN5 signature segregates progressive and regressive lesions (AUC = 1) (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1), whereas CIN70 and CIN25 signatures are somewhat poorer predictors of progression (Figure 6—figure supplement 2) (AUC = 0.82 and 0.81, respectively).
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis results presented in the text and figures, and citation to Teixeira et al., 2019.

claim: CIN70 and CIN25 signatures are poorer predictors of progression in cohort GSE108124 with AUC values of 0.82 and 0.81, respectively.
source: Cohort GSE108124 focuses on CIS lesions with known progressive potential. As reported in that study (Teixeira et al., 2019), we found that the CIN5 signature segregates progressive and regressive lesions (AUC = 1) (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1), whereas CIN70 and CIN25 signatures are somewhat poorer predictors of progression (Figure 6—figure supplement 2) (AUC = 0.82 and 0.81, respectively).
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis results presented in the text and figures.

claim: In cohort GSE114489, CIN5 has an AUC of 0.72 for segregating persistent from regressive dysplasias.
source: Furthermore, cohort GSE114489, which also contains dysplastic samples with known progression potential, demonstrates that although signatures are elevated in persistent dysplasias, neither CIN5 (AUC = 0.72) (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 3) nor CIN70 (AUC = 0.74) and CIN25 (AUC = 0.73) (Figure 6—figure supplement 4) could accurately segregate persistent from regressive samples as efficiently as CIN5 in the GSE108124 cohort.
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis results presented in the text and figures.

claim: In cohort GSE114489, CIN70 and CIN25 have AUC values of 0.74 and 0.73, respectively, for segregating persistent from regressive dysplasias.
source: Furthermore, cohort GSE114489, which also contains dysplastic samples with known progression potential, demonstrates that although signatures are elevated in persistent dysplasias, neither CIN5 (AUC = 0.72) (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 3) nor CIN70 (AUC = 0.74) and CIN25 (AUC = 0.73) (Figure 6—figure supplement 4) could accurately segregate persistent from regressive samples as efficiently as CIN5 in the GSE108124 cohort.
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis results presented in the text and figures.

claim: CIN-scores did not accurately segregate regressive from persistent/progressive samples by progression status in the discovery cohort of GSE109743.
source: Similarly, CIN-scores did not accurately segregate regressive from persistent/progressive samples by progression status in the discovery cohort of GSE109743 (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis results presented in the text and figures.

claim: In cohorts with multiple stages represented (GSE109743 and GSE33479), there was a clear increase in CIN-scores with increasing PML grade.
source: However, in cohorts with multiple stages represented (GSE109743 and GSE33479), there was a clear increase in CIN-scores with increasing PML grade (Figure 6D and E, Figure 6—figure supplement 7), which is consistent with the increased risk of malignant progression in high-grade lesions.
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis results presented in the text and figures.

claim: Inactivation of the tumour suppressor genes TP53 and CDKN2A are the most frequent somatic events in LUSC.
source: Inactivation of the tumour suppressor genes TP53 and CDKN2A (Figure 7A) are the most frequent somatic events in LUSC (Jamal-Hanjani et al., 2017; The Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two published studies (Jamal-Hanjani et al., 2017; The Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network, 2012) and reference to Figure 7A.

claim: The squamous differentiation, PI3K/Akt, and oxidative stress response are the most frequently targeted pathways in LUSC.
source: The squamous differentiation, PI3K/Akt, and oxidative stress response are the most frequently targeted pathways in LUSC (The Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to The Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network, 2012.

claim: The most frequent alteration targeting the squamous differentiation pathway is SOX2 amplification.
source: The most frequent alteration targeting the squamous differentiation pathway is SOX2 amplification, although inactivations of NOTCH proteins have also been proposed to target this pathway as they are mutually exclusive with SOX2 amplification.
evidence: The claim is stated as a fact about LUSC genetics.

claim: Inactivations of NOTCH proteins are mutually exclusive with SOX2 amplification.
source: The most frequent alteration targeting the squamous differentiation pathway is SOX2 amplification, although inactivations of NOTCH proteins have also been proposed to target this pathway as they are mutually exclusive with SOX2 amplification.
evidence: The claim is stated as a fact about LUSC genetics.

claim: The signature scores of the squamous differentiation, PI3K/Akt, and oxidative stress response pathways increased significantly in either moderate or severe dysplasias when compared with normal normofluorescent mucosa in cohort GSE33479.
source: When GSE33479 was interrogated, the signature scores of the three pathways increased significantly in either moderate or severe dysplasias when compared with normal normofluorescent mucosa.
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis results from the GSE33479 cohort.

claim: No significant increases in squamous differentiation, PI3K/Akt, and oxidative stress response pathway signatures were detected in mild dysplasias or earlier lesions in cohort GSE33479.
source: No significant increases were detected in mild dysplasias or earlier lesions.
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis results from the GSE33479 cohort.

claim: The CDK4/cyclin-D1 signature showed a significant increase in moderate dysplasias and later stages in cohort GSE33479.
source: The CDK4/cyclin-D1 signature showed a significant increase in moderate dysplasias and later stages in cohort GSE33479 (Figure 7E) and in mild dysplasias and later stages in the GSE109743 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis results presented in the text and Figure 7E.

claim: The CDK4/cyclin-D1 signature showed a significant increase in mild dysplasias and later stages in cohort GSE109743.
source: The CDK4/cyclin-D1 signature showed a significant increase in moderate dysplasias and later stages in cohort GSE33479 (Figure 7E) and in mild dysplasias and later stages in the GSE109743 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis results presented in the text and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The increase of E2F signature was detectable in metaplasias and later stages in the GSE33479 cohort.
source: The increase of E2F signature was already detectable in metaplasias and later stages (Figure 7F) in the GSE33479 cohort, whereas in the GSE109743 cohort the increase in the E2F signature was observed starting in mild dysplasias (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis results presented in the text and Figure 7F.

claim: The increase in the E2F signature was observed starting in mild dysplasias in the GSE109743 cohort.
source: The increase of E2F signature was already detectable in metaplasias and later stages (Figure 7F) in the GSE33479 cohort, whereas in the GSE109743 cohort the increase in the E2F signature was observed starting in mild dysplasias (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis results presented in the text and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The activity of squamous differentiation, PI3K/Akt, and oxidative stress response pathways start in the transition between high- and low-grade lesions, typically moderate and severe dysplasias.
source: Overall, these results show that the activity of squamous differentiation, PI3K/Akt, and pathways start in the transition between high- and low-grade lesions (Figure 1), typically moderate and severe dysplasias, indicating a role of these pathways in this transition, whereas their function in earlier stages (e.g., transition from normal epithelium to low-grade PMLs) is likely to be more limited.
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis results and inference from the observed patterns.

claim: The function of squamous differentiation, PI3K/Akt, and oxidative stress response pathways in earlier stages (e.g., transition from normal epithelium to low-grade PMLs) is likely to be more limited.
source: Overall, these results show that the activity of squamous differentiation, PI3K/Akt, and pathways start in the transition between high- and low-grade lesions (Figure 1), typically moderate and severe dysplasias, indicating a role of these pathways in this transition, whereas their function in earlier stages (e.g., transition from normal epithelium to low-grade PMLs) is likely to be more limited.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observed data patterns.

claim: The onset of CDK4/cyclin-D1 and E2F pathways start in earlier stages (metaplasias and mild dysplasias).
source: Our observations with the CDK4/cyclin-D1 and E2F signatures indicate that the onset of this pathways start in earlier stages (metaplasias and mild dysplasias).
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis results from the study.

source: The most novel aspect of this application is the emphasis on preinvasive disease (to our knowledge, the first bioinformatic tool focusing on PMLs), and the possibility of multiple sample stratifications by parameters that correlate with high risk of malignant progression (stage, progression status, and CIN).
evidence: The claim is stated by the authors based on their knowledge of existing tools.

claim: XTABLE allows multiple sample stratifications by parameters that correlate with high risk of malignant progression (stage, progression status, and CIN).

source: Regardless, CIN gene expression signatures present a very robust correlation with genomic instability indexes in cancer, and specifically in lung cancer (Carter et al., 2006).

source: For instance, SOX2 overexpression has a negative effect in cell fitness in multiple experimental scenarios (Cho et al., 2013; Correia et al., 2017; Cox et al., 2012; Wuebben et al., 2016).

source: High-grade PMLs frequently undergo malignant progression (Ishizumi et al., 2010) and therefore, detection of these lesions and removal is an optimal strategy to prevent deaths by LUSC.

claim: Detection of high-grade PMLs and removal is an optimal strategy to prevent deaths by LUSC.
